title: The Library of Alexandria didn’t vanish in one great fire
body: The popular image is a single catastrophic blaze that wiped out ancient knowledge. Historians instead see a slow decline over several centuries, driven by political purges, war damage and dwindling royal support. Many works survived elsewhere because scholars kept copying them, while others were lost simply because nobody recopied them before the papyrus decayed.

items: Fire spreads from Caesar’s burning ships
The tale of Caliph Umar’s book-burning
slides.explanation: Ptolemy VIII’s purge: 145 BC. Caesar’s fire: 48 BC. Aurelian: AD 272. The Umar story is set in 642 but appears only centuries later and is regarded as a myth.

slides.heading: 145 BC: scholars expelled
slides.text: Ptolemy VIII purged intellectuals from Alexandria. The head librarian, Aristarchus of Samothrace, fled to Cyprus, and the Library’s prestige began to slide.

slides.heading: 48 BC: Caesar’s fire
slides.text: During a siege, fire spread from burning ships in the harbor. Ancient writers say scrolls were lost, but the Library apparently survived or was soon rebuilt.

slides.heading: AD 272: war in the city
slides.text: Emperor Aurelian’s forces, retaking Alexandria from Queen Zenobia’s army, destroyed the palace quarter where the main Library had stood.

slides.heading: A later legend
slides.text: Stories that Caliph Umar ordered the books burned in 642 appear only centuries later, and historians such as Bernard Lewis regard them as a myth.
